---
title: What is an ontology?
---

```{r setup, include = FALSE}
library(ontologySpecR)
```

You do not need any background in knowledge graphs or semantic web
standards to use this package. This page explains the idea with everyday
analogies, then shows the same idea in a few lines of R.

## The floor plan analogy

Imagine a hospital where every department keeps its own map of the building.
Reception draws wards as boxes, facilities draws pipes and wiring, and the
fire team draws exits. Each map is correct for its owner, and none of them
agree on what a "room" is.

An **ontology** is the shared floor plan. It says which kinds of things exist
(rooms, wards, doors), how they relate (a ward *contains* rooms), and what you
are allowed to do with them (*lock* a door). Every team can still add its own
layers, but they all start from the same description of the building.

> **Think of it like this:** data is the furniture, an ontology is the floor
> plan. You can move the furniture daily without redrawing the plan.

## Why a written description beats tribal knowledge

Most data projects do not fail because the data is wrong. They fail because
two people mean different things by the same word, and nobody wrote it down.

`ontologySpecR` gives you a small, precise vocabulary for writing it down, in
R code, and a JSON format so the description can be shared, versioned and
checked by machines.

## The building blocks

Each block below has a plain-English role and a constructor in the package.

### Object types: the nouns

An **object type** describes a kind of real-world thing: an airport, a
patient, an invoice. It lists the thing's properties and says which property
uniquely identifies one instance (the **primary key**).

```{r object_type}
airport <- object_type(
  id = "Airport",
  properties = list(
    property_def("airport_id", "string", nullable = FALSE),
    property_def("name", "string"),
    property_def("latitude", "number"),
    property_def("longitude", "number")
  ),
  primary_key = "airport_id",
  source_kind = "table",
  source_table = "airports"
)
airport
```

The `source_*` fields say where the rows live. The description is
**backend-agnostic**: it points at a table but does not care which database
holds it.

### Link types: the verbs

A **link type** is a named relationship between two object types. A flight
route *departs from* an airport; an airline *operates* a route.

```{r link_type}
route_origin <- link_type(
  id = "RouteOrigin",
  from = "FlightRoute",
  to = "Airport",
  cardinality = "many-to-one",
  join_from_keys = "origin_id",
  join_to_keys = "airport_id"
)
route_origin
```

### Interfaces: "anything with a plug"

An **interface** is a shape contract. A travel adaptor does not care whether
it is plugged into a kettle or a laptop, only that there are two pins. In the
same way, a map component only needs "something with a latitude and a
longitude", not specifically an airport.

```{r interface}
geo_located <- interface_type(
  id = "GeoLocated",
  required_properties = list(
    property_requirement("latitude", "number"),
    property_requirement("longitude", "number")
  )
)
geo_located
```

### Actions and queries: doing and asking

- An **action type** declares an operation (for example *update airport
  status*), its parameters, and what it changes.
- A **query** is a saved, parameterised question (for example *airports within
  50 km of here*).

Both are descriptions. The package records *what* exists; other packages in
the ecosystem decide *how* to run them.

### Concepts: the adjectives

A **concept** is a named judgement about an object, written as a SQL boolean
expression: "a *busy* airport is one with more than 50,000 passengers a day".
Concepts are **versioned** and **scoped**, so two teams can define "busy"
differently without overwriting each other, and a definition can change
without silently rewriting history.

```{r concept}
busy_airport <- concept_def(
  id = "busy_airport",
  object_type_id = "Airport",
  scope = "operations",
  version = 1L,
  sql_expr = "daily_passengers > 50000",
  rationale = "Matches the operations team's staffing threshold."
)
busy_airport
```

A **concept template** is the same idea with blanks to fill in
(`utilisation_rate > {{threshold}}`), for families of similar definitions.

## Bundles: the box it all ships in

All of these blocks are packed into one **bundle**: a versioned, validated,
serialisable package of the whole ontology.

```{r bundle}
b <- bundle(
  bundle_id = "aviation-demo",
  bundle_version = "0.1.0",
  objects = list(airport),
  links = list(route_origin),
  interfaces = list(geo_located),
  concepts = list(busy_airport)
)
b
```

A bundle is just data. It can be written to one JSON file, checked against a
schema, committed to git and read by any tool that understands the format.

## Spec, not runtime

`ontologySpecR` only **describes**. It never touches a database and never runs
an action. That separation is deliberate: every other package in the
ecosystem reads the same bundle and adds one capability.

| Package | Adds |
|---|---|
| `ontologySpecR` | The shared vocabulary and file format (this package) |
| `objectSetsR` | Lazy queries over object types |
| `actionTypesR` | Running actions |
| `vertexR` | Graph analysis |
| `conceptR` | Evaluating and governing concepts |
| `objectExplorerR` | A point-and-click browser |

## The key insight

Write the description once, in one place, and let every tool read it. When
the definition of "busy airport" changes, you change one versioned entry, not
five dashboards.

## Quick reference

| Term | In plain English | Analogy |
|---|---|---|
| Object type | A kind of thing | A noun |
| Property | One field on a thing | An attribute |
| Primary key | What makes one instance unique | A passport number |
| Link type | A relationship between kinds of things | A verb |
| Interface | A shape several types can share | A plug standard |
| Action type | A declared operation | A button |
| Query | A saved question | A bookmark |
| Concept | A versioned yes/no judgement | An adjective |
| Bundle | Everything, packaged | A shipping box |
